regenerable_on: a guest running unbound with a control socket the capture user can reach, AND a daemon that has answered some queries. A freshly started resolver reports every counter as zero, which replays and diffs perfectly while teaching nothing — the first capture taken here was exactly that. The figures below are this daemon's own traffic, so a re-stage moves all of them and the anchors are re-read by hand in the same change, or they are asserting a machine that is gone.
anonymisation_note: Through the gate, and no substitution was needed. Both documents are the daemon reporting on itself — a release string, its own thread and module counts, its own uptime and pid, and counters of the queries it answered — so there is nothing here that correlates one machine or names anything an operator chose. The field says the gate ran, not that values were rewritten; harness/scrub/unbound.json states the bound under which that classification holds, and the independent detectors were run over the committed bytes afterwards.
note:
One resolver, two documents, ONE row. `status` and `stats_noreset` are separate commands on separate connections and they feed a single daemon object, so a port that published a row per document — or that keyed the collection on the command — gets a different commit count from the same payloads.

The second command is the whole reason this collector is safe to run: plain `stats` ZEROES every counter as a side effect of reporting it, so a collector wired to it would silently destroy the numbers of anything else reading the same daemon, and each reading would be a delta whose window nobody declared. `stats_noreset` reads and leaves. That is a property of the COMMAND, not of the parser, so it is captured here rather than argued for in a comment: the payload's name is the evidence that the right one was asked.

What the figures are: counters since the daemon started, never rates. The agent holds no previous sample and a collector that exits cannot remember one, so a client derives rates across the window it actually observed. 21 queries, 13 of them answered from cache and 8 that needed recursion — 13 + 8 = 21, which is the arithmetic a reader checks and a specimen should therefore hold. RecursionTimeAvgSeconds is unbound's own precomputed average, not a figure derived here.

Stated bounds, because a specimen shows one machine on one day.

The daemon runs ONE thread, so `thread0.num.queries` and `total.num.queries` are the same number on every line of the payload — and so are the other five. This capture therefore cannot tell a port that reads the `total.` prefix from one that reads whichever line matched last, which on a multi-threaded resolver are different answers about the machine. A capture from a resolver with `num-threads: 2` is what closes it.

Prefetch is off, which is unbound's default and not a fault: `total.num.prefetch=0` is present and zero, so the anchor asserts a READING rather than an absence — a port that dropped zero-valued counters as uninteresting fails it. The same holds for RequestListCurrent: the resolver is idle at the moment of capture and 0 is what idle looks like, not a missing member.

The socket answered, so this variant exercises no failure path at all. Absent, unauthorised and unavailable — no socket, a socket the collector's group cannot open, a socket with nothing listening — are three different statements the collector must make and no committed capture stages any of them. They are the live comparator's to adjudicate and an absent variant's to pin.

And the row carries values only: no names family, no absent list, no unobservable record, no relation assertion. Every fact the collection publishes is present in these two documents, so the three non-value channels are unvisited here.
anchors_note:
Read off payloads/status.txt and payloads/stats_noreset.txt by hand at staging, before any stream existed, which is what makes them an authority the reference-generated half is not.

The object is named `unbound` because that is the row's native name — the id the adapter mints is `daemon:unbound` and the collator derives it from the declared `daemon` prefix and this name, so an anchor on the id would be asserting the collator's work rather than the collector's.

Version and Uptime come from `status`, which is a `key: value` document, and the six counters come from `stats_noreset`, which is `key=value`. That difference is anchored by having both kinds present: a port that ran one parser over both files finds no `=` in the first and no `: ` in the second, and publishes half a row.

Uptime is 3648 read from the line `uptime: 3648 seconds`. The field is two tokens and only the first is the number, so a port that took the whole field fails, and one that kept it as the string "3648" fails typed equality — which the corpus judge applies precisely because a typed consumer sees the difference and `==` does not.

CacheHits 13 and CacheMiss 8 are anchored separately and deliberately differ. They are adjacent lines with near-identical keys, and two values that happened to be equal would let a port that read the wrong one pass.

RecursionTimeAvgSeconds 0.120223 is the only non-integer in the row, and it is the anchor that catches a whole class: a port that parsed every stats value as an integer publishes 0, and one that carried the token as a string publishes "0.120223". Both are wrong on the wire and both are invisible to an untyped comparison.

commit_objects 1 is the count of resolvers these two documents describe, and it is anchored because absence is not the only way to lose a collection: a port that emitted one row per document, or a row per counter, satisfies every fact anchor above and reports a different number here.

Deliberately not anchored: `time.now`, `time.up` and `time.elapsed`, the three lines at the foot of the stats document. They are readings of the clock rather than of the resolver, no fact is lifted from them, and anchoring one would pin this pair to a wall-clock moment that a re-stage cannot reproduce.
